ai.definition: Atomic assemblers are theoretical devices capable of manipulating matter at the atomic scale by placing individual atoms into desired positions with extreme precision.
ai.howItWorks: These devices would theoretically employ scanning tunneling microscope (STM) or similar tip-based techniques to move and position atoms one by one, allowing for the construction of precise molecular structures from the ground up.
ai.problemSolved: Precision manufacturing at the atomic level; creation of materials with tailored properties beyond current capabilities.
ai.manufacturing: Theoretically involves complex nanoscale manipulation processes that are currently beyond practical implementation.
ai.buildProcess: Requires advanced STM technology or similar, as well as precise control systems and possibly cryogenic conditions to maintain atomic stability.
ai.costDrivers: High development costs due to cutting-edge research; potential for expensive materials and equipment needed for initial prototypes.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Long-term vision with significant technical challenges to overcome before practical implementation.
ai.regulation: No current regulations apply as the technology is purely theoretical, but future development could require new regulatory frameworks.
ai.risks: High risk due to unproven technology and potential for unforeseen physical or chemical limitations at the atomic scale.
ai.profitability: Uncertain; depends on successful commercialization of applications in manufacturing and medicine.
ai.futureDevelopment: Potential for breakthroughs in nanotechnology, quantum computing, and material science if theoretical concepts are realized.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units would draw low hundreds to a few watts; fabrication processes would be energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and precise control systems.

glossary.def: The scale of individual atoms, typically on the order of picometers (10^-12 meters).
A type of scanning probe microscope that can image surfaces at atomic resolution and manipulate atoms.

subsystems.name: Manipulator tips
subsystems.role: Pick up, position and bond individual atoms or molecules.

subsystems.name: Positioning stage
subsystems.role: Move each tip with sub-atomic precision in three dimensions.

subsystems.name: Control and sensing
subsystems.role: Determine where atoms are and guide each reaction step.

subsystems.name: Feedstock delivery
subsystems.role: Supply the right atoms or molecules to each tip in the right order.

subsystems.name: Environment enclosure
subsystems.role: Keep out contaminants and hold a stable, cold, vibration-free vacuum.

subsystems.name: Product design and simulation
subsystems.role: Specify the atomic layout of the target and the reaction pathway to build it.

subsystems.name: Thermal management
subsystems.role: Remove heat from exothermic bond-forming reactions at the nanoscale.

buildSteps.title: Design the product and the tooling
buildSteps.detail: Map every atom and bond in the target object, and work out a sequence of reactions that builds it without unwanted side reactions.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the first manipulator molecules
buildSteps.detail: Use existing chemical methods to make tip molecules that can selectively bind and release specific atoms.

buildSteps.title: Position a single manipulator
buildSteps.detail: Use a scanning probe microscope to place one manipulator tip and image its position before each operation.

buildSteps.title: Demonstrate mechanosynthesis
buildSteps.detail: Use the tip to form simple bonds one at a time — for example, adding a carbon atom to a growing molecule — and verify the result.

buildSteps.title: Bootstrap replication
buildSteps.detail: Design a manipulator that can build copies of itself from simple feedstock molecules, so the system can grow.

buildSteps.title: Scale to parallel arrays
buildSteps.detail: Replicate many manipulators and arrange them in dense arrays on a chip-like substrate, each independently positioned and controlled.

buildSteps.title: Operate the factory
buildSteps.detail: Feed in feedstock, run programmed sequences across the array, and harvest atomically precise products.

buildSteps.title: Maintain and error-correct
buildSteps.detail: Continuously monitor for misplaced atoms and bonds, and correct errors before they propagate.

prerequisites.tech: Scanning probe microscopy and single-atom manipulation
prerequisites.why: Scanning tunnelling and atomic force microscopes can already image and move individual atoms, though very slowly.
Some experiments have used probe tips to form or break specific bonds, but no general, programmable method exists.
One tip is far too slow for manufacturing; thousands working in parallel without interference is unsolved.
A system that can make copies of its own manipulators from simple feedstock is theoretical.
Any practical assembler must detect and fix misplaced atoms at rates far beyond current capability.
Molecular simulation can suggest pathways, but predicting and controlling complex sequences remains hard.

pathway.milestone: single-atom manipulation and synthesised molecular machines in the laboratory
pathway.unlocks: basic tools and proof that atoms can be positioned on demand.

pathway.milestone: mechanosynthesis of small molecules using scanning probes
pathway.unlocks: a general method for making and breaking chosen bonds with a tip.

pathway.milestone: self-assembling molecular components that form nanoscale structures
pathway.unlocks: cheap production of atomically precise parts without assembling every atom individually.
throughput high enough to build useful macroscopic objects.
bottom-up fabrication of a wide range of materials and devices.
